modules.d: AI won't replace teachers — but teachers who use AI will redefine the profession. Your new role.
modules.body:
The question every teacher is asking — answered honestly

"Will AI replace teachers?" No — but it will transform what teaching is. The parts of the job a machine can do (drafting, differentiating, grading routine work, generating materials) are being automated. The parts only a human can do (inspiring, mentoring, reading a child's face, building character) become more valuable, not less. The AI-era educator offloads the mechanical and pours the reclaimed time into what actually changes lives. This course makes you that educator.

"Technology will not replace great teachers, but technology in the hands of great teachers can be transformational." — George Couros. AI is the most powerful such technology yet — and it lands in your hands, not over your head.

What AI gives back to teachers: time

Teacher burnout is largely a time problem — hours lost to prep, paperwork, and grading that never touch a student. AI is, above all, a time machine for educators:

  • Lesson planning in minutes, aligned to your curriculum and objectives.
  • Differentiation — the same lesson instantly leveled for different readers and needs.
  • Materials — worksheets, quizzes, examples, rubrics, parent letters — on demand.
  • Feedback — faster, richer, more consistent (with your judgment on top).
  • Admin — emails, reports, and documentation drafted for you.

Reclaim those hours and spend them where the magic is: with students.

The educator's non-negotiables (Commandments, applied to teaching)

  • You are the professional. AI drafts; you decide. Every material is checked by your expertise and judgment before it reaches a student.
  • Accuracy matters doubly in education. A hallucinated fact taught as truth is a real harm. Verify — Commandment 2 is sacred in the classroom.
  • Protect students. Never put student personal data or identifiable work into public AI tools without consent and care (Module 3 goes deep). Do no harm.
  • Model good use. How you use AI teaches your students how they should — integrity, transparency, and thinking with the tool, not outsourcing to it.
The mindset shift: stop seeing AI as either a threat to resist or a cheat to fear. See it as a tireless teaching assistant who preps, differentiates, and drafts on command — while you remain the teacher who inspires, judges, and cares. The assistant handles the mechanical so the human can be more human.

Going deeper — what the evidence says about AI in classrooms

Early research on AI in learning shows a consistent pattern: design decides outcomes. A widely cited field experiment in Turkish high schools (Bastani et al.) found that students given unrestricted access to a GPT-4 tutor performed better during practice but worse on later exams without it than students who never had it, while a version designed with teacher-written hints that withheld direct answers largely avoided that harm. A World Bank–supported after-school pilot in Nigeria, where students used AI with teacher guidance, reported substantial learning gains over six weeks. The lesson: AI that gives answers can replace thinking; AI designed to prompt thinking can support it.

  • Productive struggle: learning needs effort. Design AI use so students attempt first and get hints, not solutions.
  • Teacher in the loop: the strongest results come when teachers frame tasks, set guardrails and debrief.
  • Equity: unequal access to devices and connectivity can widen gaps. Plan for offline and shared-device options.
UNESCO guidance recommends a human-centred approach, age-appropriate use, data protection, and building teacher capacity before scaling. Check your national and school policies too.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an instructional designer. I teach [subject, level, setting]. Design one AI-supported activity that requires students to attempt the task first, then use AI only for hints, then explain their reasoning without AI. Include the student-facing prompt rules, a no-device alternative, and how I'll debrief.

📚 Glossary

  • Productive struggle: Effortful thinking that builds durable learning
  • Teacher in the loop: Teacher designs, guides and reviews AI use
  • Digital divide: Unequal access to devices and connectivity
  • Human-centred AI: Using AI to support, not replace, human agency

📖 References

  • Bastani, H. et al. (2024/2025). Generative AI can harm learning. Working paper; published in PNAS (2025) as 'Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning'.
  • De Simone, M. et al. (2025). From chalkboards to chatbots: evaluating the impact of generative AI on learning outcomes in Nigeria. World Bank Policy Research Working Paper.
  • UNESCO (2023). Guidance for generative AI in education and research.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Offload the mechanical, protect the human. The clearer you are on this line, the more AI helps without hollowing out your craft.
  • You are always the professional. AI drafts; your expertise decides what reaches a child.
  • Model integrity. How you use AI quietly teaches your students how they should.

📚 Glossary

  • Differentiation: adapting the same content to different learners' levels and needs.
  • AI-era educator: a teacher who offloads mechanical work to focus on human impact.
  • Human-in-the-loop: teacher judgment reviewing every AI output.

📖 Explore further

  • UNESCO — AI in education guidance.
  • Ethan Mollick & Lilach Mollick on teaching with AI — One Useful Thing.

quiz.q: Mrs. Ngwa, a Grade 6 teacher in Bamenda, spends about 9 hours a week on worksheets, parent letters and marking quizzes. She wants AI to cut burnout without weakening her teaching. Which plan best fits the course's AI-era educator model?
opts: Use AI to write her lesson delivery scripts while she keeps worksheet and letter writing in her own hands
Let AI mark and return all quizzes directly so she can spend the saved hours preparing new lesson content
Keep every task manual this term and pilot AI next year once the school has a formal policy in place
Have AI draft worksheets and letters, review each, and put saved hours into small-group mentoring
quiz.x: The model is: offload mechanical drafting, review it, and reinvest time in human work with students. The runner-up (AI marks and returns quizzes) removes her review step and spends the time on more prep rather than students.

quiz.q: A Houston middle-school teacher asks AI for a short history reading. It states confidently that a treaty was signed in 1848 when the real date was 1846. She has 20 minutes before class. What should she do?
opts: Check the key dates against a reliable source, correct the text, then hand it out to the class
Hand it out as written and plan to mention in class that AI texts sometimes contain small errors
Discard the reading and teach the lesson from memory without any handout this time
Ask the same chatbot to double-check its own dates and use whichever version it gives second
quiz.x: Accuracy matters doubly in teaching: a hallucinated fact taught as truth is real harm, so she verifies against a reliable source. Asking the chatbot to re-check itself is a tempting runner-up but the same model can repeat or invent errors.

quiz.q: A head teacher in Douala wants to type pupils' full names, home addresses and behaviour notes into a free public chatbot to draft end-of-term letters to parents. What is the most appropriate response under the course's non-negotiables?
opts: Go ahead but delete the chat history afterwards so the personal details are not kept by the provider
Go ahead, as long as each letter is checked carefully by a teacher before it is sent to the family
Draft a placeholder template in the chatbot, then add each pupil's details offline
Use the chatbot with first names and behaviour notes but leave out the home addresses of the pupils
quiz.x: Student personal data should not go into public tools without consent and care; placeholders keep the time saving while protecting pupils. Removing only addresses is the runner-up but still exposes identifiable names and sensitive behaviour notes.

quiz.q: Mr. Fon must decide a Form 4 pupil's final report-card judgment, and also produce a leveled version of a text for three reading groups. Using the lab's offload-or-keep logic, how should he split the work?
opts: Keep both fully human, since any AI involvement in a child's records would undermine trust in him
Offload a draft of the leveled texts to AI for review, and keep the report-card judgment fully human
Keep the leveled texts human because reading levels matter, and let AI draft the report-card comment
Offload both to AI as drafts, then review both carefully before anything reaches the pupil or parents
quiz.x: Leveling a text is mechanical drafting that AI does well under review; a final judgment about a child stays human. Drafting both with review sounds balanced but the course places final judgments on a child entirely with the teacher.

quiz.q: In the Bastani et al. field study in Turkish high schools, one group had an unrestricted GPT-4 tutor and another a version with teacher-written hints that withheld answers. What pattern did the study report?
opts: Both AI groups improved exam scores equally, showing that tutor design made little difference to outcomes
Practice scores rose with the unrestricted tutor but exam scores later fell; the hint version mostly avoided this
Neither group's practice scores changed, but both groups' exam scores rose modestly versus the control
The unrestricted tutor raised exam scores most, while the hint version slowed learning down for students
quiz.x: The study found practice gains but about a 17% drop in later exam scores for unrestricted use, while teacher-designed hints avoided most harm: design decides outcomes. The equal-improvement option is the common misconception that any AI access helps.

quiz.q: A school board in Yaoundé reads that UNESCO estimates the world needs 44 million additional teachers by 2030 and proposes replacing some teacher posts with AI tutors. Which response best reflects the course?
opts: AI tutors can fill much of the gap in sub-Saharan Africa if they are deployed in every secondary school
The gap is best closed by having AI teach core subjects while teachers handle discipline and welfare
AI cannot fill that gap, but freeing existing teachers' time from paperwork helps the teachers we have
The figure is mainly a European problem, so it says little about staffing needs in Cameroon schools
quiz.x: The course states AI cannot fill the gap, and that sub-Saharan Africa holds the largest share; AI's role is reclaiming teachers' time. Deploying AI tutors everywhere is the plausible-sounding runner-up that ignores the human roles AI cannot replace.

quiz.q: A Nigerian after-school pilot supported by the World Bank ran for 6 weeks and reported substantial learning gains. A district officer wants to copy it by simply giving pupils chatbot access at home. What is the key flaw?
opts: The pilot paired AI with teacher guidance; removing the teacher changes the intervention itself
The gains came from the specific chatbot brand, so the district must buy exactly the same product
Home use is better than school use because pupils can practise longer, so the copy should work even better
Six weeks is too short for any gains to be real, so the district should wait for a full-year study first
quiz.x: The teacher-in-the-loop design is the point, not the tool alone, echoing the Bastani finding. Doubting the six-week length is a defensible caution but misses why copying without teachers changes the result.

quiz.q: Ms. Johnson in Atlanta lets students see her use AI to draft a quiz, then shows how she checked and edited it. A colleague says this 'gives students ideas to cheat'. Which non-negotiable is she actually applying?
opts: You are the professional: editing in public proves to parents that she makes the final decisions
Protect students: keeping AI visible in class prevents pupils from using unsafe tools at home in secret
Accuracy first: by checking the quiz openly she reduces the chance of any errors reaching her class
Model good use: open, critical use of the tool teaches students how they should use it
quiz.x: How you use AI teaches students how they should, so open, critical use is modelling. Accuracy first is the runner-up since she does verify, but the point of doing it in front of students is modelling, not just error-catching.

quiz.q: A teacher says: 'AI is either a threat I must resist or a cheating machine I must police.' According to the mindset shift in Module 1, how should she reframe it?
opts: As a tireless assistant that preps and drafts while she inspires, judges and cares
As a replacement for routine teaching that lets her focus mainly on discipline and administration
As a neutral tool best kept out of class until students are old enough to handle it responsibly
As a cheating risk to be managed with detectors, while she uses it privately for her own planning
quiz.x: The course frames AI as a teaching assistant handling the mechanical so the teacher can be more human. Using detectors plus private use is the runner-up, but Module 3 shows detectors are unreliable and it keeps the threat mindset.

quiz.q: A principal in Bafoussam asks: if a teacher reclaims 5 hours a week with AI over a 36-week school year, how many hours could go back to students, and what does the course say to do with them?
opts: About 180 hours; spend them producing more worksheets and materials so every lesson has extra practice
About 41 hours; spend them on training to become an AI specialist for the rest of the school staff
About 41 hours; spend them on extra administrative reporting that the ministry increasingly expects
About 180 hours; spend them on mentoring, feedback conversations and reading how each child is doing
quiz.x: 5 x 36 = 180 hours, and the course says to reinvest reclaimed time where the magic is: with students. More materials is the runner-up, but it pours the time back into the mechanical work AI was meant to absorb.

facts.t: Drop in later exam scores for students given an unrestricted GPT-4 tutor (Turkey field study).
facts.more: Bastani et al. found practice scores rose, but exam scores without AI fell versus students who never had it. A version with teacher-written hints that withheld answers largely avoided the harm: design decides outcomes.

facts.t: Length of the World Bank–supported after-school AI pilot in Nigeria.
facts.more: Students used AI with teacher guidance and the pilot reported substantial learning gains. The teacher-in-the-loop design is the point, not the tool alone.

facts.t: Additional teachers UNESCO estimates the world needs by 2030.
facts.more: Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for the largest share. AI cannot fill that gap, but reclaiming teachers' time from paperwork helps the teachers we have.

facts.t: …you decide. The first educator's non-negotiable.
facts.more: Every AI-generated material passes your expertise before reaching a student. A hallucinated fact taught as truth is a real harm (Commandment 2).

modules.body:
Where AI saves teachers the most time

Lesson planning and differentiation are the biggest, most repetitive time-sinks in teaching — and where AI delivers the most dramatic relief. This module gives you reusable workflows (not one-off tricks) that turn an evening of prep into a few minutes of directing and reviewing. Build these once and use them every week for the rest of your career.

Workflow 1 — The curriculum-aligned lesson plan

The key is giving AI your real context, not a generic ask. A strong lesson-plan prompt includes: the topic, the grade/level, your learning objectives (ideally your exact curriculum standards), the time available, your students' context, and the format you want. Feed all of that and you get a plan you can actually teach — then you refine it with your judgment.

Objectives first. The single biggest quality lever is giving AI your specific learning objectives or standards. "Plan a lesson on fractions" is weak. "Plan a 45-minute lesson for Grade 5 meeting objective [X: compare fractions with unlike denominators], with a hook, guided practice, and an exit ticket" is a plan you can walk into class with.

Workflow 2 — Instant differentiation

This is AI's superpower for inclusive teaching. Take one lesson or text and instantly adapt it:

  • By reading level: "Rewrite this passage at three levels — below, at, and above grade — keeping the same core content."
  • For support needs: "Adapt this for a student who needs simpler language and shorter chunks."
  • For extension: "Add two challenge questions for students who finish early."
  • For language learners: "Provide a version with key vocabulary defined in simple terms."
  • By interest: "Reframe these word problems around football / music / cooking to boost engagement."

What used to mean writing three versions of everything by hand now takes one prompt — real differentiation becomes finally achievable for a busy teacher.

Workflow 3 — The materials factory

From one lesson, generate the whole supporting set: a worksheet, a short quiz, a rubric, worked examples, discussion questions, and a parent update — all aligned and on demand. Save your best prompts (Level 2's prompt library) so next week is even faster.

"Differentiation is the hardest thing we ask of teachers, and the first thing that gets cut when time runs out." AI removes the time barrier — for the first time, meeting every learner where they are is realistic on a normal teaching schedule.

🧪 Lesson-plan lab (copy → run to plan a real lesson)

You are an expert instructional designer. Plan a [duration] lesson on [topic] for [grade/level]. Learning objective(s): [your exact standard/objective]. Student context: [class size, needs, language]. Include: a hook, direct instruction, guided practice, an independent task, and an exit ticket. Then differentiate the independent task into three versions (below / at / above level), and list the materials I'll need. Ask me one clarifying question first if anything essential is missing.

Going deeper — differentiation that respects learners

AI makes it easy to produce three versions of every task. Use that power carefully:

  • Differentiate access, not expectations. Adjust reading level, scaffolds, vocabulary support and format, while keeping the same core learning objective for all. Permanently giving some students easier goals can lower attainment.
  • Universal Design for Learning (UDL): offer multiple means of engagement, representation and expression — e.g. a diagram plus text, choice of written or oral response.
  • Avoid labels: don't name tiers "low/high". Use neutral labels or let students choose their starting scaffold.
  • Check accuracy and bias: simplified texts can drop key facts or introduce errors; AI examples may default to cultural contexts unfamiliar to your students. Localise names, currencies and settings.
Prompt pattern: "Create three versions of this reading for grade 7: one at a grade-5 reading level with a glossary, one at grade level, one with an extension question. Keep the same key facts and the same learning objective: [objective]. Use Cameroonian names and settings." Then check each version against the original.

Curriculum alignment

Always paste the actual curriculum objective or competency statement. Without it, AI plans drift toward generic content that may not match your national programme or exam.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a curriculum specialist. Here is my national curriculum objective: [paste]. Create a lesson plan with a starter, main activity, three differentiated access versions (same objective), a UDL option for expression, a quick formative check, and local examples from [country]. Then list anything I must verify for accuracy.

📚 Glossary

  • Differentiation: Adapting instruction to learners' needs
  • UDL: Universal Design for Learning: multiple means of engagement, representation and expression
  • Scaffold: Temporary support that helps learners reach a goal
  • Formative check: A quick assessment during learning to guide teaching

📖 References

  • CAST (2024). Universal Design for Learning Guidelines 3.0. udlguidelines.cast.org

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Objectives are the quality lever. Paste your exact standards; generic asks give generic lessons.
  • Build a workflow, not a one-off. Save your best planning and differentiation prompts to reuse weekly.
  • Differentiation is finally realistic. One prompt replaces three hand-written versions — use it every lesson.

📚 Glossary

  • Learning objective/standard: the specific skill a lesson targets.
  • Exit ticket: a quick end-of-lesson check of understanding.
  • Differentiation: adapting content to different learners.
  • Materials factory: generating a full aligned set from one lesson.

📖 Explore further

  • Teacher-focused tools (verify current features): MagicSchool, Diffit, Khanmigo, Brisk.
  • Level 2's prompt-library habit makes these workflows compound.

quiz.q: Mr. Tabi in Buea types 'Plan a lesson on fractions' and gets a generic plan. He teaches a 45-minute Grade 5 class. Which revision to his prompt will improve the plan most, according to the module?
opts: Add a request for a longer, more detailed plan with more activities so he can choose from a wider range
Add the exact objective (compare fractions with unlike denominators) plus hook, practice, exit ticket
Add his students' favourite sports and music so the examples feel more relevant to the class in Buea
Add a role line such as 'you are a world-class maths teacher' and ask the model to think step by step
quiz.x: Specific learning objectives are the single biggest quality lever. Adding student interests is a useful runner-up (context helps) but without a clear objective the plan still lacks focus.

quiz.q: A teacher in Chicago has one science passage and three reading groups. She asks AI to rewrite it at three levels. What should she keep identical across the three versions?
opts: The reading level of the questions, while varying how much of the passage each group receives
The number of questions and their difficulty, while varying which topic each group is studying
The core content and learning objective, while varying language, scaffolding and challenge
The vocabulary list and sentence length, while varying the content covered by each reading group
quiz.x: Standard differentiation keeps content and objective the same and changes language, scaffolding and challenge. Varying content per group is the common misconception that turns differentiation into tracking.

quiz.q: In a Yaoundé class, Amina finishes early every day. Pierre is still learning French, the language of instruction. Which pairing of AI moves matches the module's differentiation lab?
opts: Amina: add more practice items at the same level; Pierre: rewrite the passage at a lower reading level
Amina: add extension questions climbing Bloom's levels; Pierre: define key vocabulary in simple terms
Amina: rewrite the passage at a higher level; Pierre: translate the whole lesson into English for him
Amina: reframe the problems around her interests; Pierre: add challenge questions to keep him engaged
quiz.x: Early finishers get challenge or extension that climbs the levels; language learners get key vocabulary support. 'More of the same' for Amina and simpler reading level for Pierre is the runner-up, but extension should climb levels and Pierre's need is language, not reading ability.

quiz.q: A teacher asks AI to tag each of her 8 quiz questions by revised Bloom's level. It labels 'List the three states of matter' as 'Analyse'. What should she conclude and do?
opts: The tag is a minor issue, since Bloom's levels matter mainly for university courses, not schools
The tag is wrong; listing is 'Understand', so she should ask AI to regenerate the whole quiz
The tag is acceptable, because recalling three states requires analysing the differences between them
The tag is wrong; listing is 'Remember', so she checks every tag rather than trusting the labels
quiz.x: Listing facts is the 'Remember' level, and the module says ask AI to tag levels then check it. Calling it 'Understand' is the close runner-up but misplaces recall one level too high.

quiz.q: Mr. Eto'o's Form 2 class in Garoua is disengaged with word problems, but most pupils follow football closely. Which AI prompt best applies the module's 'by interest' differentiation?
opts: Rewrite these word problems at a lower reading level so disengaged pupils can follow them
Add two harder challenge problems so the more able pupils stay motivated during the lesson
Reframe these word problems around football while keeping the same maths skills and difficulty
Replace these word problems with football trivia questions so pupils enjoy the lesson more
quiz.x: Interest-based reframing changes the context but keeps the skill and level. Lowering the reading level is the runner-up but addresses a reading need, not the engagement problem described.

quiz.q: A teacher in Lagos uses the 'materials factory' workflow. From one lesson on photosynthesis, which set of outputs best shows the workflow used correctly?
opts: An aligned worksheet, quiz, rubric and parent update, each reviewed, with the prompt saved for reuse
A single long handout combining notes, quiz and answers, so parents and pupils have everything at once
A complete set of materials generated fresh each week, so the prompts do not become stale or repetitive
A worksheet and quiz generated separately in two different tools, so the class sees more variety
quiz.x: The factory produces an aligned set from one lesson and saves the best prompts to reuse. Generating fresh each week sounds energetic but discards the reusable-workflow benefit the module stresses.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian teacher has a class where some pupils' home language is Pidgin or a national language, while lessons are in English. What does the module suggest is a key differentiation move here?
opts: Provide versions with key vocabulary defined in simple terms, keeping the same lesson content
Teach the main lesson in Pidgin and summarise in English so every pupil follows the key content
Place these pupils in a separate group studying a simplified curriculum until their English improves
Use AI translation of every handout into each home language so no English vocabulary is needed
quiz.x: The module highlights simple vocabulary support for language learners while keeping core content. Full translation into each home language is the runner-up, but it is rarely accurate for low-resource languages and removes language-of-instruction practice.

quiz.q: Two teachers plan the same lesson. Teacher A writes a 2-line prompt; Teacher B includes topic, grade, objectives, time, student context and format. B's plan needs 10 minutes of editing, A's needs 40. Over 30 lessons, how much time does B's approach save?
opts: About 20 hours, because each plan needs 40 fewer minutes of editing across 30 lessons
About 12 hours, because each plan needs 25 fewer minutes of editing across 30 lessons
About 5 hours, because each plan needs 10 fewer minutes of editing across 30 lessons
About 15 hours, because each plan needs 30 fewer minutes of editing across 30 lessons
quiz.x: 40 - 10 = 30 minutes saved per lesson; 30 x 30 = 900 minutes = 15 hours. The 20-hour figure is the runner-up error of using A's full 40 minutes instead of the difference.

quiz.q: A US teacher asks AI for extension tasks for advanced readers. AI returns ten more recall questions of the same type. Using the module's Bloom's guidance, what is the best fix?
opts: Keep the ten questions but add a time limit so advanced readers are pushed to work faster
Ask AI to rewrite the passage at a higher reading level and reuse the original question set
Ask for tasks climbing to analyse, evaluate and create, like critiquing the author's argument
Ask for twenty recall questions instead, since advanced readers can handle a heavier workload
quiz.x: Extension should climb the levels, not add more of the same. A harder text is a defensible runner-up but keeps questions at recall level.

quiz.q: A teacher wants to differentiate weekly but has little time. She builds a strong leveling prompt once. What does the module recommend she do next?
opts: Share the outputs with colleagues but keep the prompt private so her method stays distinctive
Save it in her prompt library and reuse it each week, refining it as she learns what works
Rewrite a new prompt each week so the AI does not produce repetitive material for pupils
Use it for a month and then switch to a different AI tool to compare which one levels better
quiz.x: The module stresses reusable workflows: build once, save in the prompt library, and reuse weekly. Writing a new prompt each week is the runner-up but throws away the time savings.

facts.t: Your specific learning objectives are the biggest quality lever in a lesson-plan prompt.
facts.more: 'Plan a lesson on fractions' is weak; a 45-minute Grade 5 lesson meeting a named objective with hook, guided practice and exit ticket is teachable.

facts.t: Revised Bloom's taxonomy: remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, create.
facts.more: Ask AI to tag each question by level — then check it. Extension tasks should climb the levels, not just add more of the same.

facts.t: Below, at and above level: the standard differentiation split.
facts.more: Keep the core content and objective identical across versions; change the language, scaffolding and challenge.

facts.t: Official languages in Cameroon: English and French.
facts.more: Many classes also include learners whose home language is a national language or Pidgin. Simple vocabulary support is a key differentiation move.

The teacher's AI toolkit (2025–26)

Beyond the general chatbots, a whole category of education-specific AI tools has emerged, built around teacher workflows and (crucially) student-data safety. This module maps the landscape so you pick the right tool per job. Tools evolve fast — verify current features, pricing, and privacy terms before adopting one for real student use.

Purpose-built teacher platforms

  • MagicSchool: a broad teacher suite — dozens of tools for planning, materials, feedback, IEP support, and more, designed around school workflows and privacy. Great one-stop starting point.
  • Diffit: specializes in exactly Module 1's superpower — take any text/topic and instantly generate leveled reading passages with questions and vocabulary. A differentiation powerhouse.
  • Khanmigo (Khan Academy): an AI tutor for students and a teaching aid, notable for a Socratic style that guides learners rather than handing answers — and for its safety-first design.
  • Brisk / others: browser-extension tools that work on top of Google Docs/Classroom for feedback and material creation inside the platforms teachers already use.

The general tools, in a teaching role

  • Claude / ChatGPT / Gemini: maximum flexibility for planning, drafting, and ideation — your CLEAR prompting makes them do almost anything. Best when a purpose-built tool doesn't fit.
  • NotebookLM: grounded Q&A over YOUR sources — upload the textbook chapter and curriculum, and get cited, on-syllabus answers and study aids (including audio overviews for revision). Excellent for accuracy.
  • Canva / Ideogram: visuals, posters, and slide design for engaging materials.
"Purpose-built for privacy" is the phrase that matters in education. The reason to prefer a teacher platform over a raw chatbot for student work isn't features — it's that it's designed to handle student data responsibly. Module 3 makes this non-negotiable.
Choosing fast — a teacher's decision rule: leveled reading passages → Diffit. A broad all-in-one with privacy → MagicSchool. A guided student tutor → Khanmigo. Cited answers from your own textbook → NotebookLM. Open-ended planning & drafting → a general model (Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini). Anything involving identifiable student data → a tool cleared by your school's privacy policy, never a random free app.

Going deeper — student data privacy and age rules

Before using any AI tool with students, check three things:

  • Age requirements: many general chatbots set minimum ages (often 13, with parental consent required below 18 for some services). Purpose-built education platforms may offer student accounts designed for younger learners under school control.
  • Data protection: in the US, FERPA and COPPA govern student records and children's data; in Europe, GDPR applies with stricter rules for children; Cameroon's 2024 law on personal data protection also sets obligations. Check whether the vendor signs a data agreement, whether student data trains models, and where data is stored.
  • Teacher-facing vs student-facing: a tool used only by teachers to plan (no student data entered) carries much lower risk than one where students log in or upload work.
Never paste student names, grades, special needs details or behaviour records into a consumer chatbot. Anonymise: "Student A, grade 8, reading two years below grade level".

Evaluating a teacher platform

Score candidates on: curriculum fit, output quality (test five real tasks), privacy terms, cost and offline access, language support (English/French), and whether it saves you time after review. Free tiers and features change often — recheck before committing a school.

modules.d: Faster, richer feedback — plus honest strategies for a world where students have AI too.
modules.body:
Two hard problems AI reshapes at once

Assessment is where AI both helps teachers enormously (faster, richer feedback) and creates a genuine challenge (students have AI too). This module handles both honestly: how to use AI to give better feedback, and how to design assessment with integrity in the AI era — not by fighting a losing detection war, but by rethinking what and how we assess.

AI-assisted feedback (with you in charge)

  • Faster first-pass feedback: "Give specific, encouraging feedback on this essay against this rubric, noting two strengths and two priorities." You then personalize and verify — the human touch stays yours.
  • Consistency: AI applies a rubric evenly across a class, reducing fatigue-driven drift — you spot-check and adjust.
  • Richer than a grade: generate actionable next steps, not just a score — what to do to improve, specifically.
  • Feedback in students' language: translate or simplify feedback for language learners.
The line you never cross: AI can draft feedback and apply a rubric, but the teacher owns the final judgment — especially for high-stakes grades and anything on a permanent record. And never paste identifiable student work into a non-approved tool (Module 2's privacy rule). AI assists the feedback; you remain the assessor.

Academic integrity: stop fighting, start redesigning

AI detectors are unreliable and produce false accusations — a dead end. The durable answer is to design assessment that AI can't simply do for the student, and to teach honest AI use openly:

  • Assess the process, not just the product: drafts, outlines, revisions, and reflections show the thinking AI can't fake for them.
  • In-class and oral components: discussion, presentation, and live explanation reveal genuine understanding.
  • Make it personal and local: tasks tied to a student's own experience, your specific classroom, or current local context are hard to outsource.
  • Raise the cognitive bar: ask for analysis, critique, application, and synthesis — not retrieval a chatbot hands over.
  • Teach AI use openly: set clear, honest rules for when and how AI may be used, and require students to disclose it — turning a threat into a skill.
"If an AI can complete your assignment perfectly, the problem may be the assignment." — a hard but freeing truth. The AI era is pushing assessment toward what always mattered most: thinking, process, and understanding over regurgitation.

🧪 Redesign lab (copy → run on one of your assignments)

You are an assessment-design expert for the AI era. Here is one of my current assignments: [paste it]. First, tell me honestly how easily a student could complete it with AI. Then redesign it to assess genuine understanding — incorporating process (drafts/reflection), a personal or local element, and a higher-order thinking demand (analysis/critique/application) — while keeping it fair and doable. Finally, suggest a clear, honest AI-use policy statement I can put on the assignment.

Going deeper — why detectors fail and what works instead

AI-text detectors are unreliable for high-stakes decisions. OpenAI withdrew its own classifier in 2023 for low accuracy, and a Stanford study (Liang et al.) found detectors misclassified a large share of essays by non-native English writers as AI-generated. Accusing a student based on a detector score risks serious unfairness.

  • Assess process, not just product: drafts, outlines, version history, in-class writing and short oral check-ins ("talk me through your argument").
  • Set clear AI-use levels per task: e.g. an AI Assessment Scale ranging from no AI, to AI for planning, to AI for editing, to full AI collaboration with reflection. Students should know exactly what's allowed.
  • Design authentic tasks: local data, personal experience, recent events, and applied problems are harder to outsource.
  • Require AI disclosure: a short statement of what AI was used for and how the student checked it.
Feedback with AI, decisions by you. AI can draft rubric-aligned comments quickly, but teachers should review every comment and keep grading decisions human. Students value feedback that shows the teacher read their work.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an assessment designer. Here is an assignment I set: [paste]. Redesign it for the AI era: specify the permitted AI-use level, add one process checkpoint and a short oral check-in, make it more authentic using local context, and write the student AI-disclosure statement. Then draft a rubric with four criteria.

📚 Glossary

  • AI detector: Tool that estimates whether text was AI-generated; unreliable for decisions
  • AI Assessment Scale: Framework defining permitted levels of AI use per task
  • Authentic assessment: Tasks rooted in real contexts and applied problems
  • Process evidence: Drafts, notes and history showing how work was produced

📖 References

  • Liang, W. et al. (2023). GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers. Patterns.
  • Perkins, M., Furze, L., Roe, J. & MacVaugh, J. (2024). The AI Assessment Scale. Journal of University Teaching and Learning Practice.

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Don't rely on detectors. They're unreliable and risk false accusations — redesign instead.
  • Assess the process. Drafts, reflections, and oral defenses reveal thinking AI can't fake for a student.
  • Teach honest use openly. Clear rules plus disclosure turn AI from a threat into a taught skill.

📚 Glossary

  • Formative feedback: guidance to improve, not just a grade.
  • AI-resilient assessment: tasks that require genuine, hard-to-outsource thinking.
  • Process assessment: grading drafts, revisions, and reflection.
  • AI-use policy: explicit rules for when/how students may use AI.

📖 Explore further

  • Level 1's integrity Commandments and Level 2's judgment principles apply directly.
  • UNESCO & university teaching centers publish evolving AI-integrity guidance — check current best practice.

quiz.q: A teacher in Kumba runs an essay through an AI detector, which reports '87% AI-written' for a bilingual student. What is the most defensible next step?

Report the case for misconduct, since a score above 80% is strong enough evidence

quiz.x: Detectors are unreliable and penalise non-native writers, so a score cannot justify an accusation. A second detector is the runner-up, but two unreliable tools do not make reliable evidence.

quiz.q: Liang et al. (2023) tested seven AI detectors on TOEFL essays by non-native English writers. What did they find, and why does it matter for Cameroon's bilingual classrooms?

An average of 61% were wrongly flagged as AI, so bilingual learners face false accusations
Detectors were accurate for non-native writers but failed with essays written by native speakers
Native-speaker essays were flagged most often, so bilingual learners are relatively protected
quiz.x: Liang et al. found an average 61% false flag rate on non-native essays, with native essays rarely flagged. 26% is a real figure from the module, but it is OpenAI's classifier's correct-detection rate, not this study.

quiz.q: OpenAI's own AI-text classifier was withdrawn in 2023. According to the module, what share of AI-written text did it correctly flag?
opts: About 26%, and it also mislabelled some human text as AI-written
About 61%, and it rarely mislabelled human writing as AI-written
About 74%, but it struggled with texts by non-native English writers
About 90%, but it was withdrawn over cost rather than accuracy
quiz.x: The classifier caught only about 26% of AI text and produced false positives. 61% is the Liang et al. false-flag figure for non-native essays, a common mix-up.

quiz.q: A teacher uses the AI Assessment Scale. For a research project, she wants AI for brainstorming but not for writing. What is the main benefit of stating the permitted level per task?
opts: It lets detectors be calibrated to each level, so cheating can be caught more reliably
Students know exactly what is allowed, and disclosing AI use becomes a normal habit
It removes the need for process evidence, since students agree to the level in advance
It lets the teacher ban AI on most tasks, which keeps grading simpler for everyone
quiz.x: The scale's five levels tell students what is allowed and normalise disclosure. Removing the need for process evidence is a tempting runner-up, but process evidence is still how understanding is shown.

opts: Return the grades as they are, since even rubric application is the main fairness goal
Spot-check a sample, adjust where AI misread work, and confirm high-stakes grades herself
Re-mark every script by hand, since any AI involvement makes the grades unreliable
Ask students to report errors after release, then correct the grades that were wrong
quiz.x: AI reduces drift, but the teacher spot-checks and owns final judgment, especially for high-stakes grades. Re-marking every script is the cautious runner-up but wastes the benefit; spot-checking is what the module asks.

An analysis of a local Bamenda market problem using interviews done in class
An oral defence where each student explains choices in their own project
A take-home task to define ten listed science terms in full sentences
quiz.x: Take-home definitions are pure retrieval a chatbot hands over. The local analysis is the runner-up candidate for 'easy', but personal, local and in-class elements make it hard to outsource.

quiz.q: A teacher wants to translate feedback into simpler French for a language learner and save the result in the school's records. What rule must she keep while doing this?
opts: Use an approved tool and avoid pasting identifiable student work into non-approved ones
Ask the student to translate it themselves, since AI translation of feedback is unreliable
Use any free translator, since translation does not count as processing student data
Translate just the grade, not the comments, so the meaning stays exactly as she wrote it
quiz.x: Feedback in students' language is encouraged, but identifiable work must not go into non-approved tools. Claiming translation is not data processing is the misconception here.

quiz.x: The module calls for raising the cognitive bar and adding personal, local and oral elements. Moving retrieval questions into class is a defensible runner-up but still assesses recall, not thinking.

The most important thing you'll teach this decade

Your students will spend their entire lives and careers alongside AI. Teaching them to use it wisely, critically, and ethically may be the most consequential thing you do — more lasting than any single subject. AI literacy isn't a computing topic; it's a life skill, like reading or reasoning, and every teacher in every subject can build it. This module shows how.

"We are not preparing students for our past; we are preparing them for their future." That future is saturated with AI. A student who can direct AI thoughtfully — and spot its failures — holds a decisive advantage; one who can't is left behind. You decide which your students become.

The four pillars of student AI literacy

  • Understanding (what AI is): age-appropriately, that AI is a powerful pattern-tool trained on data — not magic, not a person, not always right. Demystify it.
  • Critical evaluation (trust wisely): the vital habit of questioning AI output — checking for hallucinations, bias, and missing perspectives. This is the new critical thinking.
  • Effective use (direct it well): basic prompting and knowing which tasks AI helps with — and which need a human. Your own CLEAR skills, taught down to their level.
  • Ethical use (do right): honesty about when AI was used, respecting others' work, protecting privacy, and understanding fairness and bias. Character in the AI age.

How to build it in ANY subject

  • History: have AI write an account, then students fact-check and find its bias — critical evaluation in action.
  • Science: use AI to generate a hypothesis or explanation, then test and critique it.
  • Language arts: co-write with AI, then discuss what the student added that AI couldn't — voice, truth, experience.
  • Any subject: "AI got this wrong — find the error" is a powerful, transferable exercise that builds healthy skepticism.
The teach-the-limits principle: the single most valuable AI-literacy lesson is showing students where AI fails — the confident hallucination, the biased answer, the missing viewpoint. A student who expects AI to be fallible uses it wisely; one who trusts it blindly is vulnerable. Make "check it" a reflex.

🧪 Literacy-lesson lab (copy → run to design an activity)

You are a curriculum designer for AI literacy. Design a [duration] activity for my [grade/subject] class that builds one AI-literacy pillar — [understanding / critical evaluation / effective use / ethical use]. Tie it to my subject content: [topic]. Include a hook, the student task, a “find where AI got it wrong” element to build healthy skepticism, and a short discussion to close. Keep it age-appropriate and doable with the tools I have.

Going deeper — a progression for AI literacy

AI literacy frameworks (UNESCO's AI competency framework for students, 2024; the joint EU/OECD AI literacy framework draft, 2025) converge on a few strands. Build them progressively:

  • Understand: AI learns patterns from data; it predicts, it doesn't "know". It can be wrong, biased and confident at the same time.
  • Use: prompt clearly, iterate, and choose when AI helps and when it doesn't.
  • Evaluate: verify claims against sources; spot hallucinations, bias and deepfakes.
  • Create: make things with AI responsibly — with attribution and disclosure.
  • Reflect on ethics and society: privacy, fairness, jobs, environmental cost, and who benefits.
Unplugged activities work. Students act as a "language model" predicting the next word from a pile of sentences; a "biased training set" sorting game using only pictures of one group; a fact-check race against an AI answer. No devices needed, and the concepts stick.

Age guidance

Younger students: concepts and unplugged activities, teacher-led demonstrations. Lower secondary: guided use with clear rules and verification tasks. Upper secondary: independent use with disclosure, critical projects on AI in society. Follow your school's and tools' age policies.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an AI literacy curriculum designer. My students are [age, subject, setting, device access]. Design a four-lesson mini-unit covering understand, use, evaluate, create and ethics, including at least one unplugged activity, one verification challenge, and one discussion on AI in our local community. Include learning objectives and a final task.

📚 Glossary

  • AI literacy: Knowledge and skills to understand, use and evaluate AI responsibly
  • Unplugged activity: Teaching a computing concept without devices
  • Deepfake: Synthetic media realistic enough to deceive
  • Training data: Examples a model learns patterns from

📖 References

  • UNESCO (2024). AI competency framework for students.
  • European Commission & OECD (2025). Empowering learners for the age of AI: an AI literacy framework (draft).

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Teach the limits first. “Find where AI got it wrong” builds the skepticism that protects students for life.
  • Any subject can build literacy. You don't need a computing class — history, science, and language arts all work.
  • Model it yourself. Your transparent, critical AI use is the most powerful lesson of all.

📚 Glossary

  • AI literacy: understanding, critically evaluating, using, and ethically applying AI.
  • Critical evaluation: questioning AI output for errors, bias, and gaps.
  • Healthy skepticism: expecting AI to be fallible and checking it.

📖 Explore further

  • UNESCO — AI competency frameworks for students.
  • Level 1's data & vocabulary modules translate directly into student lessons.

quiz.q: A history teacher in Bamenda has AI write an account of the 1961 reunification, then asks students to fact-check it and identify its bias. Which literacy pillar does this mainly build?
opts: Critical evaluation, by questioning AI output for errors, bias and missing views
Ethical use, by teaching students to disclose when they have used AI tools
Understanding, by showing students how AI generates text from training data
Effective use, by teaching students to write clearer prompts for history topics
quiz.x: Fact-checking and finding bias is critical evaluation in action. Understanding is the runner-up but explaining how AI works is a different activity from testing its output.

quiz.q: A Grade 4 teacher in Atlanta wants to explain, at her pupils' level, why chatbots can sound sure but be wrong. Which explanation best fits the module?
opts: It searches the internet for each answer, so its mistakes come from websites that are wrong
It is a kind of digital person who sometimes guesses when it is tired or confused
It predicts likely words from patterns it learned, so it can sound right without being right
It copies answers from a big database of facts, which sometimes has out-of-date entries
quiz.x: Language models predict likely text from training data, which explains confident errors. 'It searches the internet' is the common misconception, since many models generate rather than look up.

quiz.q: A secondary school wants one AI literacy lesson that will transfer across all subjects. According to the teach-the-limits principle, which activity is most valuable?
opts: A talk on AI history from the 1956 Dartmouth workshop to the present day
A prompting workshop where students learn to get the best answers fast
A demonstration of the most impressive AI tools so students see their power
'AI got this wrong: find the error' tasks that build a habit of checking
quiz.x: Showing where AI fails is the single most valuable literacy lesson. The prompting workshop builds effective use, a valid pillar, but without the checking reflex students trust output blindly.

quiz.q: A language arts teacher in Lagos has students co-write a story with AI, then discuss what the students added that AI could not. What does this activity draw out?
opts: The right prompt format, so students can get finished stories in one attempt
The student's own voice, truth and lived experience as distinct from the AI's text
The grammar rules AI follows, so students can copy its sentence structures
The speed advantage of AI, so students learn to draft more quickly in exams
quiz.x: The module's language arts example asks what the student added that AI could not: voice, truth, experience. Prompt format belongs to effective use but misses the point of the activity.

quiz.q: A student submits a project and writes: 'I used AI to suggest an outline, then wrote and checked everything myself.' Which pillar is she demonstrating?
opts: Effective use, by picking a task where AI helps
Critical evaluation, by checking the content AI produced for her
Understanding, by knowing that AI is a pattern tool, not a person
Ethical use, through honesty about when and how AI was used
quiz.x: Disclosing AI use honestly is part of ethical use. Effective use is a close runner-up since she picked a sensible task, but the act shown here is the disclosure.

quiz.q: A maths teacher says AI literacy is the computing teacher's job, not hers. What does the module argue?
opts: It belongs mainly in computing, though other teachers may support it
It is a life skill like reading or reasoning that every subject can build
It should wait until upper secondary, when students are mature enough
It is best taught by outside AI specialists invited for special sessions
quiz.x: AI literacy isn't a computing topic; it is a life skill every teacher can build. 'Mainly computing, others support' is the runner-up that sounds reasonable but contradicts the module's stance.

quiz.q: A science teacher uses AI to propose a hypothesis about why seedlings in a Yaoundé classroom grew unevenly, then has students test and critique it. Which two pillars does this build most directly?
opts: Critical evaluation and effective use, via testing output and a suitable AI task
Ethical use and critical evaluation, by respecting authorship and checking for bias
Understanding and ethical use, by learning how AI works and disclosing its role
Understanding and effective use, by learning AI's history and practising prompts
quiz.x: Testing and critiquing AI's hypothesis is critical evaluation; using AI to generate a hypothesis is effective use. Understanding plus effective use is the runner-up, but no lesson on how AI works is involved.

quiz.q: A parent complains that teaching children 'AI is often wrong' will make them afraid of technology. Which reply best reflects the module?
opts: The message is temporary, because AI errors will disappear as the tools keep improving
Children should avoid AI until they are older, so the warning simply prepares them for that
Students who expect AI to be fallible use it wisely, while blind trust makes them vulnerable
Children respond better to fear, so stressing AI's failures helps them stay away from it
quiz.x: Teaching the limits builds healthy skepticism and wise use, not fear. Saying errors will disappear is the hopeful runner-up, but it encourages the blind trust the module warns against.

quiz.q: A teacher explains that 'artificial intelligence' became a field's name at a 1956 workshop. Why does the module suggest this kind of history?
opts: To demystify AI as decades of research, not magic, which builds understanding
To honour the scientists who invented AI, which builds ethical use
To inspire students to become AI researchers, which builds effective use
To show that AI has long been unreliable, which builds critical evaluation
quiz.x: The 1956 Dartmouth workshop shows AI is not new or magic; demystifying is the Understanding pillar. Linking it to critical evaluation sounds plausible but the purpose is demystification.

quiz.q: A teacher designs a 40-minute AI literacy activity for Form 1. The module's lab template asks for several elements. Which plan includes them?
opts: A video on AI history, a worksheet of definitions, and a class rule to distrust chatbots
A demonstration of three AI tools, free exploration time, and a vote on the most useful one
A short lecture on AI risks, a quiz on key terms, and a take-home prompt-writing assignment
A hook, a subject-linked task, a find-the-error element, and a closing discussion
quiz.x: The lab asks for a hook, a subject-tied task, a find-where-AI-got-it-wrong element and a short closing discussion. The lecture-quiz-assignment plan is the runner-up but lacks the error-finding element.

facts.t: Understanding, critical evaluation, effective use, ethical use.
facts.more: AI literacy is a life skill every subject can build, not only a computing topic.

facts.more: AI is not new or magic: it is decades of research into pattern-learning systems. Demystifying starts with history.

facts.t: The teach-the-limits principle: show students where AI fails.
facts.more: A student who expects AI to be fallible uses it wisely; one who trusts it blindly is vulnerable.

Bring it all together for your real classroom

Your capstone isn't theoretical — it's a real, usable teaching artifact you'll actually deploy: a complete unit, a set of workflows, or a classroom AI system built with everything from this course. The test is simple: does it save you time, serve your students better, and uphold integrity and privacy? If yes, you've become an AI-era educator — and you have the materials to prove it.

Choose your capstone track

  • The Complete Unit: a full multi-lesson unit — curriculum-aligned plans, differentiated materials for at least three learner levels, AI-assisted feedback tools, and an AI-resilient assessment with an honest AI-use policy.
  • The Teacher Workflow System: your reusable prompt library and toolkit for planning, differentiation, materials, and feedback — documented so a colleague could adopt it.
  • The AI-Literacy Mini-Course: a sequence of activities that builds all four literacy pillars in your students, tied to your subject.
  • The Inclusive Classroom Kit: a differentiation system that adapts your core content for every learner — language, level, and need.

Capstone requirements

  • Real and usable — something you'll actually use, not a demo.
  • Curriculum-aligned — tied to your real objectives/standards.
  • Genuine differentiation — evidence of meeting varied learners.
  • Integrity & privacy by design — an AI-use policy and safe handling of student data (Modules 2–3).
  • Your prompt log — the CLEAR prompts you used, with iterations — proving the transferable skill.
  • A short reflection — what it saves you, how it helps students, and where you kept human judgment central.
"The teacher who uses AI won't replace the teacher who doesn't — but they will redefine what's possible in a classroom." Your capstone is that redefinition made concrete: more time for students, better support for every learner, and integrity intact.
🎓 Certification. Passing every module (75%+) and completing your capstone earns the AI Unlocked: Education certificate — a print-ready PDF with a QR validation code, signed by Innocent Forteh, Program Director, Team21 Academy. Each module also carries its own certificate in your Certificates tab.
Lead onward. Take these skills further with Level 2 OPERATE (build automations and systems for your whole school), Vibe Coding (build a custom classroom tool), or the Servant Leadership program (lead other educators through the AI transition). The AI-era educator is also an AI-era leader.
🧪 Capstone planner (copy → run to design your unit/system)

You are my capstone advisor for an AI-enabled classroom. My context: [grade, subject, class, constraints]. Help me choose the strongest track (complete unit, workflow system, AI-literacy mini-course, or inclusive kit). Then build a plan: the curriculum objectives it targets, how it differentiates for at least three learner levels, the AI-assisted feedback approach, an AI-resilient assessment with an honest AI-use policy, and how I'll protect student privacy. Finish with exactly what my finished, usable submission must contain.

🧪 Validated exercise

A capstone must protect student data — handling privacy and integrity by ___.

Going deeper — proving your capstone works

A capstone that "saves time and serves students better" must show evidence of both. Plan a simple before/after:

  • Time: log planning and marking time for one week without your AI workflow and one week with it (including review time).
  • Learning: use a short pre-check and post-check aligned to the unit objective, or compare with a similar previous class. Even small samples, honestly reported, are valuable.
  • Student voice: three questions — what helped, what confused you, how did you use AI? Their answers often reveal integrity or access issues you missed.
  • Integrity and privacy check: confirm no identifiable student data went into non-approved tools, and that each task states its AI-use level.
Make it shareable. Package your capstone so a colleague could use it tomorrow: a one-page overview, the prompts (with variables), materials, the AI-use rules for students, and your evidence. Sharing builds your reputation as the school's AI lead.

Reflection prompts

What did AI do well? Where did you overrule it? Which students benefited most and least, and why? What will you change next term?

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a teacher-researcher mentor. Here is my AI-enabled unit and the evidence I collected (time logs, pre/post checks, student comments): [paste]. Summarise the evidence honestly, identify which students benefited most and least, check the integrity and privacy safeguards, and suggest one change for next term.

📚 Glossary

  • Pre/post check: Short assessments before and after a unit to measure learning
  • Student voice: Students' own feedback on their learning experience
  • Net time saved: Time saved minus time spent reviewing AI output
  • Teacher-researcher: Teacher who systematically studies their own practice

💡 Tips & hidden unlocks

  • Build what you'll actually use. A real next-unit beats an impressive hypothetical.
  • Your prompt log is the proof. It shows the transferable skill, not just the output.
  • Design integrity in. An AI-use policy and safe data handling are requirements, not extras.

📚 Glossary

  • Capstone: the real, usable teaching artifact that completes the course.
  • By design: integrity and privacy built in from the start.
  • Prompt log: your documented, iterated CLEAR prompts.

📖 Explore further

  • Continue with Level 2, Vibe Coding, or Servant Leadership.
  • Share your capstone with the Team21 community — team21online@gmail.com.

quiz.q: Ms. Achu, a Grade 8 English teacher in Buea, wants a capstone she will use this term. She has three ability bands and struggles most with prep time. Which track fits best?
opts: The AI-Literacy Mini-Course, since literacy is the most important skill this decade
The Complete Unit, with leveled materials, AI-aided feedback and AI-resilient assessment
The Teacher Workflow System, documented in detail so the whole school could adopt it
The Inclusive Classroom Kit, built as a demo she can present to the ministry next year
quiz.x: A full unit covers differentiation for three bands and feedback she can use now. The Workflow System is a strong runner-up for prep time, but a unit she teaches this term also proves differentiation and assessment.

quiz.q: A teacher's capstone has excellent differentiated lessons and an AI-use policy, but no record of the prompts used. Which requirement is missing?
opts: The curriculum alignment that ties the lessons to real objectives or standards
The privacy-by-design element showing safe handling of student data
The prompt log showing the CLEAR prompts and iterations that prove the skill
The short reflection on what it saves and where human judgment stayed central
quiz.x: The prompt log records the CLEAR prompts with iterations. The reflection is a separate requirement and is the runner-up confusion.

quiz.q: What pass mark does each module require for the AI Unlocked: Education certificate, and what else is needed?
opts: 75% or more on average, with the capstone as optional extra
70% or more on average across modules, plus the capstone
75% or more on every module, plus a completed capstone
80% or more on every module, with no capstone
quiz.x: The certificate needs 75%+ on every module plus a completed capstone. An average-based 75% is the runner-up but every module must pass.

quiz.q: A teacher in New Jersey asks whether her capstone has succeeded. Which set of three tests does the module give?
opts: Does it use many tools, include a policy, and fit within one school week?
Is it aligned, differentiated, and checked by an AI detector before use?
Is it innovative, technically advanced, and impressive to school leaders?
Does it save time, serve students better, and uphold integrity and privacy?
quiz.x: The three tests are time saved, students served better, and integrity and privacy upheld. 'Aligned and differentiated' are real requirements, but detector checks contradict Module 3.

quiz.q: A teacher builds a polished AI-literacy demo for a conference but has no plan to use it with her own class. Which capstone requirement is weakest?
opts: Real and usable: it should be something she will use, not a demo
Integrity and privacy: it should include an AI-use policy for students
Prompt log: it should record the CLEAR prompts used
Genuine differentiation: it should show evidence for varied learners
quiz.x: 'Real and usable' is the first requirement and rules out demos. Differentiation may also be missing, but the scenario's defining flaw is that it will not be used.

quiz.q: A teacher in Ebolowa writes in her reflection: 'AI wrote my report-card comments and I sent them unchanged.' Which part of the reflection requirement does this conflict with?
opts: Listing which AI tools she used and why she chose each one
Showing where she kept human judgment central in her work
Describing how the materials helped her students learn better
Explaining how much time the AI workflow saved
quiz.x: The reflection must show where human judgment stayed central, and final judgments on children are human. Time saved is part of the reflection too, but sending AI comments unchanged breaks the judgment requirement.

quiz.q: A Douala teacher's capstone serves mixed-language learners in English, French and Pidgin, adapting core content by language, level and need. Which track does it best match?
opts: The Complete Unit track
The Teacher Workflow System
The AI-Literacy Mini-Course
The Inclusive Classroom Kit
quiz.x: The Inclusive Classroom Kit adapts core content for every learner by language, level and need. The Complete Unit also differentiates, but its focus is a full multi-lesson unit with assessment.

quiz.q: A head of department wants a capstone that colleagues across the school could adopt for planning, differentiation, materials and feedback. Which track and key feature fit?
opts: Workflow System, with prompts and toolkit documented so a colleague could adopt it
Inclusive Kit, so colleagues adapt each lesson for every learner automatically
Complete Unit, with plans and materials shared on the school drive for reuse
AI-Literacy Mini-Course, so all colleagues teach the four pillars the same way
quiz.x: The Workflow System is a documented prompt library and toolkit a colleague could adopt. Sharing a Complete Unit is the runner-up, but it gives colleagues one unit rather than reusable workflows.

quiz.q: A capstone includes an AI-resilient assessment but students' names and grades are pasted into a free chatbot to draft feedback. Which requirement fails, linking to earlier modules?
opts: Genuine differentiation, since chatbot feedback treats every learner the same way
Curriculum alignment, since feedback from a chatbot may not match the standards
Integrity and privacy by design, as identifiable data went to an unapproved tool
Real and usable, since chatbot feedback cannot be used in a real classroom
quiz.x: Privacy by design (Modules 2 to 3 here) rules out pasting identifiable data into non-approved tools. Alignment is a possible secondary concern, but the clear breach is privacy.

quiz.q: After the capstone, a teacher wants to build a custom classroom tool and also help colleagues through the AI transition. Which next steps does the course suggest?
opts: Repeat the capstone on a second track, then apply to become a Team21 course mentor
Vibe Coding for the tool, and the Servant Leadership program for leading colleagues
The Servant Leadership program for the custom tool and Level 2 OPERATE for leadership
Level 2 OPERATE for the custom tool and Vibe Coding for leading the other educators
quiz.x: Vibe Coding builds custom classroom tools; Servant Leadership is for leading other educators. Level 2 OPERATE is a real option, but it is for school-wide automations, not leadership.

steps.s: Your AI-drafted unit looks complete. What do you do before teaching it?
o: Teach it as is; it looks professional and well structured
Polish hides errors; unreviewed content can teach falsehoods.
Check facts, alignment and level; edit where needed
You are the professional: AI drafts, you decide.
Ask a colleague to skim the first lesson only, to save time
Helpful, but the whole unit needs your review.

steps.s: Your differentiated versions differ: the lower level drops the main objective.
o: Restore the objective with simpler language and support
Differentiate the route, never the destination.
Keep it; weaker pupils need less content
Lowers expectations and widens gaps.
Remove the lower level and give everyone the same text
Equal, but not equitable; some learners will be lost.

steps.s: A colleague wants to adopt your workflow and asks for your prompts.
o: Share them with your notes on what worked
Documented prompts make your system transferable — a capstone goal.
Tell them to use any chatbot their own way
Loses the reliability you built.
Share only the final outputs
Useful once, but they can't reuse or adapt the process.

steps.s: A parent asks whether AI is grading their child.
o: Say AI drafts feedback; you review and decide grades
Honest and accurate — transparency builds trust.
Say AI is not used at all in your marking
Dishonest; it undermines trust when discovered.
Avoid the question and move on to the next topic
Not a lie, but evasive; transparency is better.
